items.q: A stroke patient can comprehend spoken and written commands perfectly, but speech is slow, halting, effortful, and telegraphic. Repetition is severely impaired, and the patient displays obvious frustration. Where is the lesion located?
items.exp: Broca aphasia is characterized by non-fluent, effortful expressive speech with preserved comprehension, localized to Brodmann areas 44 and 45 in the inferior frontal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere.
r: Correct. Broca expressive aphasia localizes to the dominant inferior frontal gyrus.
Incorrect. Wernicke aphasia features fluent speech with severely impaired comprehension.
Incorrect. Conduction aphasia features fluent speech with intact comprehension and isolated repetition failure.
Incorrect. Angular gyrus lesions cause Gerstmann syndrome.
items.kp: Broca aphasia localizes to the dominant inferior frontal gyrus, causing non-fluent speech with preserved comprehension.

items.q: An elderly patient speaks with normal cadence and grammar, but sentences are incomprehensible nonsense full of neologisms and paraphasic errors. The patient cannot follow simple commands and seems unaware of the communication barrier. Which cortical area is infarcted?
o: Brodmann area 22 in posterior superior temporal gyrus
Brodmann areas 44 and 45 in inferior frontal gyrus
items.exp: Wernicke aphasia is characterized by fluent but meaningless speech (word salad), impaired comprehension, and lack of awareness (anosognosia), localizing to Brodmann area 22 in the posterior superior temporal gyrus.
r: Correct. Brodmann area 22 is Wernicke area, mediating language comprehension.
Incorrect. Areas 44 and 45 constitute Broca expressive area.
Incorrect. Area 4 is primary motor cortex.
Incorrect. Area 17 is primary visual cortex.
items.kp: Wernicke aphasia is a receptive fluent aphasia with impaired comprehension localized to Brodmann area 22.

items.q: A patient presents with intact fluency, preserved auditory comprehension, but a striking inability to repeat sentences spoken by the examiner. Which anatomical white matter pathway is damaged?
items.exp: Conduction aphasia is caused by interruption of the arcuate fasciculus connecting Wernicke and Broca areas, characterized by fluent speech, normal comprehension, but severely impaired repetition.
r: Correct. Conduction aphasia stems from arcuate fasciculus white matter tract injury.
Incorrect. Corpus callosum lesions cause interhemispheric disconnection syndromes.
Incorrect. Anterior commissure connects bilateral temporal lobes.
Incorrect. Internal capsule lesions cause motor or sensory hemiparesis.
items.kp: Conduction aphasia features fluent speech, preserved comprehension, and marked repetition impairment due to arcuate fasciculus damage.

items.q: Gerstmann syndrome is characterized by agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia, and right-left disorientation. Which cortical region is damaged in the dominant hemisphere?
items.exp: Gerstmann syndrome (tetrad of agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia, right-left confusion) localizes to the angular gyrus (Brodmann area 39) of the dominant parietal lobe.
r: Correct. Dominant angular gyrus lesions produce Gerstmann syndrome.
Incorrect. Precentral gyrus lesions cause hemiplegia.
Incorrect. Superior temporal lesions cause Wernicke aphasia.
Incorrect. Cingulate lesions cause akinetic mutism or emotional blunting.
items.kp: Gerstmann syndrome (agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia, right-left disorientation) localizes to the dominant angular gyrus.

items.q: A patient with an ischemic stroke in the non-dominant (right) parietal lobe fails to dress the left side of their body, ignores visitors standing on their left side, and denies that their left arm is paralyzed. What clinical syndrome does this represent?
items.exp: Non-dominant (typically right) parietal lobe lesions cause contralateral hemispatial neglect and anosognosia (denial of illness), where patients disregard the contralateral sensory environment.
r: Correct. Non-dominant parietal lesions cause contralateral spatial hemineglect and anosognosia.
Incorrect. Kluver-Bucy syndrome results from bilateral amygdala lesions.
Incorrect. Gerstmann syndrome occurs in dominant parietal lobe lesions.
Incorrect. Anton syndrome is visual anosognosia from bilateral occipital destruction.
items.kp: Non-dominant right parietal lobe infarction leads to profound contralateral hemispatial neglect and anosognosia.

items.q: Bilateral lesions of the anterior temporal lobes including the amygdala produce hyperorality, hypersexuality, placidity, and visual agnosia. What is this clinical syndrome?
items.exp: Kluver-Bucy syndrome is caused by bilateral damage to the anterior temporal lobes including the amygdaloid nuclei, characterized by hyperphagia/hyperorality, docility, and loss of fear.
r: Correct. Bilateral amygdala/temporal destruction produces Kluver-Bucy syndrome.
Incorrect. Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome results from thiamine deficiency in mammillary bodies.
Incorrect. Balint syndrome results from bilateral parieto-occipital lesions.
Incorrect. Foster Kennedy syndrome results from olfactory groove meningioma.
items.kp: Bilateral anterior temporal lobe destruction involving the amygdala produces Kluver-Bucy syndrome.

items.q: On the motor homunculus of the precentral gyrus, where are the neurons controlling voluntary movements of the lower extremity located?
o: Medial aspect of the hemisphere along longitudinal fissure
Middle third of the precentral gyrus
items.exp: The motor homunculus is inverted: lower extremity representation lies on the medial surface within the anterior cerebral artery territory, while hands and face occupy the lateral convexity (MCA territory).
r: Correct. Lower extremity motor control occupies the medial cortex in the ACA territory.
Incorrect. Lateral convexity controls face, tongue, and hand movements.
Incorrect. Middle convexity controls trunk and shoulder.
Incorrect. Prefrontal cortex governs executive planning.
items.kp: On the motor homunculus, the lower limb is mapped onto the medial cortex, while the upper limb and face occupy the lateral convexity.

items.q: Which Brodmann area is designated as the primary motor cortex?
items.exp: Brodmann area 4 designates the primary motor cortex in the precentral gyrus, containing giant Betz pyramidal cells that project into the corticospinal tract.
r: Correct. Area 4 is the primary motor cortex.
Incorrect. Area 6 is the premotor and supplementary motor cortex.
Incorrect. Area 17 is primary visual cortex.
Incorrect. Area 44 is part of Broca motor speech area.
items.kp: Brodmann area 4 corresponds to the primary motor cortex located in the precentral gyrus.

items.q: Balint syndrome consists of optic ataxia, ocular apraxia, and simultanagnosia. It is classically produced by bilateral watershed infarctions of which cortical territory?
items.exp: Balint syndrome (triad of optic ataxia, ocular apraxia, and simultanagnosia) results from bilateral damage to the parieto-occipital association cortex, often after severe watershed hypoperfusion.
r: Correct. Bilateral parieto-occipital borderzone injury produces Balint syndrome.
Incorrect. Orbitofrontal lesions produce disinhibition and personality changes.
Incorrect. Temporal lesions cause auditory and language deficits.
Incorrect. Cingulate lesions cause akinetic mutism.
items.kp: Balint syndrome (simultanagnosia, optic ataxia, ocular apraxia) localizes to bilateral parieto-occipital borderzone cortex.

items.q: Which vascular territory supplies the primary visual cortex (Brodmann area 17) lining the calcarine sulcus?
items.exp: The calcarine branch of the posterior cerebral artery provides the primary arterial perfusion to the primary visual cortex lining the calcarine fissure on the medial occipital surface.
r: Correct. Calcarine branch of PCA supplies primary visual cortex.
Incorrect. MCA supplies lateral hemispheric convexity.
Incorrect. ACA supplies medial frontal and anterior parietal surfaces.
Incorrect. SCA supplies superior cerebellar hemisphere.
items.kp: The primary visual cortex along the calcarine fissure is supplied by the calcarine artery of the posterior cerebral artery.
